title: ABRAHAM SENT HAGAR AND HIS SON INTO THE WILDERNESS WITH BREAD AND WATER
paragraphs:
ABRAHAM SENT HAGAR AND HIS SON INTO THE WILDERNESS WITH BREAD AND WATER
She walked away carrying bread, water, and a breaking heart—but the God who seemed silent had already heard the cry that nobody else could hear.
There are Bible stories we read too quickly because slowing down would make them hurt.
Genesis 21 is one of them.
Abraham rises early in the morning.
He takes bread.
He takes a skin of water.
He gives them to Hagar.
Then he sends her away.
Not into another comfortable household.
Not into a carefully prepared future.
Into the wilderness.
And beside her is her son.
Read that slowly.
A mother.
A child.
Bread that will eventually disappear.
Water that will eventually run dry.
And behind them, the household that had once represented security growing smaller with every step.
Genesis does not invite us to pretend this scene is painless.
It is painful.
It is complicated.
And it began long before Hagar stepped into that wilderness.
It began when human beings tried to accomplish through human strategy what God had promised to accomplish by His power.
God had promised Abraham an heir. But as the years passed and Sarah remained childless, waiting became unbearable.
So Sarah gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Hagar conceived.
Ishmael was born.
And what looked like a solution became a household filled with wounds.
That is one of the frightening things about unbelief.
Sometimes it does not look like rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like problem-solving.
Sometimes it sounds reasonable.
Sometimes it even appears successful for a while.
But whenever we attempt to manufacture what God has asked us to trust Him for, the consequences can reach people we never intended to hurt.
Years passed.
Then God did what He had promised.
Sarah conceived.
Isaac was born.
The impossible child arrived because the God who makes promises is not limited by aging bodies, impossible circumstances, or exhausted human hope.
But the arrival of Isaac did not erase the consequences of what had happened before him.
At the feast celebrating Isaac's weaning, Sarah saw Ishmael behaving toward Isaac in a way that Genesis describes with the Hebrew participle מְצַחֵק — məṣaḥēq.

The word comes from the root צחק (ṣ-ḥ-q), associated with laughter. English translations render the expression differently, and the later apostolic interpretation in Galatians 4:29 describes the son born according to the flesh as persecuting the son born according to the Spirit.
Sarah demanded that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away.
Abraham was deeply distressed.
Genesis 21:11 says the matter was very grievous in Abraham's sight because Ishmael was his son.
His son.
That matters.
Ishmael was not an inconvenience to Abraham.
He was his child.
God then told Abraham not to be distressed concerning the boy and Hagar, affirming that the covenant line would be reckoned through Isaac while also promising concerning Ishmael:
כִּי־זַרְעֲךָ הוּא
ki-zar‘akha hu
“Because he is your offspring.”
God had not confused Ishmael with Isaac.
Isaac was the son through whom the covenant promise would continue.
But Ishmael was not invisible to God.
That distinction is crucial.
Election of Isaac for the covenant line did not mean divine indifference toward Ishmael.
So morning came.
Abraham took bread and water and gave them to Hagar.
Then she departed.
The Hebrew text says:
וַתֵּלֶךְ וַתֵּתַע בְּמִדְבַּר בְּאֵר שָׁבַע
vattelekh vattēta‘ bemidbar Be’er Shava
She went and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
Wandered.
There is something painfully human in that word.
Maybe you know what it feels like.
You still wake up.
Still go to work.
Still answer messages.
Still smile when somebody asks whether you are okay.
Still post photographs.
Still tell people, “God is good.”
But inside?
You are wandering.
You know how to keep moving.
You just do not know where you are going anymore.
Maybe something happened that you never imagined would become part of your testimony.
A marriage broke.
Someone betrayed you.
Your child walked away.
A ministry disappointed you.
A door closed.
Someone you prayed for died anyway.
The money disappeared.
The diagnosis came.
The person who promised to stay left.
Or maybe the wilderness was partly created by your own decisions.
That can hurt even more.
Because now you are not only suffering.
You are remembering.
“If only I had listened.”
“If only I had waited.”
“If only I had not sent that message.”
“If only I had walked away.”
“If only I had trusted God.”
Regret has a cruel way of making the wilderness feel deserved.
But Genesis 21 gives us a picture we desperately need.
The water eventually ran out.
Hagar placed her son beneath one of the shrubs.
Then she moved away.
Why?
Because she could not bear to watch him die.
The woman who had survived conflict, displacement, rejection, and wandering finally reached the place where she had nothing left to fix.
No water.
No plan.
No visible rescue.
She sat at a distance and wept.
Perhaps you have been there.
Not physically beneath a desert shrub.
But spiritually?
Absolutely.
There are moments when the strongest prayer you can produce is crying.
Moments when you have explained yourself enough.
Fought enough.
Pretended enough.
Held everybody together enough.
And now there is nothing left except tears.
Then comes one of the most beautiful sentences in this entire account.
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר
Vayyishma Elohim et-qol hanna‘ar.
“God heard the voice of the boy.”
God heard.
Before Hagar saw provision, God heard.
Before circumstances changed, God heard.
Before she knew how the story would end, God heard.
The wilderness was silent to Hagar.
But heaven was not deaf.
And there is something even deeper here.
The name Ishmael, יִשְׁמָעֵאל (Yishma‘el), carries the idea “God hears.”
The boy whose name testified that God hears was crying in a wilderness where it looked as though God had forgotten him.
But God heard him.
His circumstances had not cancelled the truth carried in his own name.
And your wilderness has not cancelled the character of God either.
You may not understand what He is doing.
You may not know why He permitted something.
You may be living with consequences that cannot simply be reversed.
But silence is not proof of absence.
Pain is not proof that God has stopped seeing.
And exhaustion is not evidence that His promises have failed.
The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven:
“What troubles you, Hagar?”
Then came the words a terrified mother desperately needed:
“Fear not.”
Why?
Because God had heard.
Then Scripture says:
וַיִּפְקַח אֱלֹהִים אֶת־עֵינֶיהָ
Vayyifqach Elohim et-‘eineha.
“God opened her eyes.”
And she saw a well of water.
Do not miss that.
The text does not say that Hagar created the well.
It says God opened her eyes and she saw it.
Sometimes grace does not arrive by giving us the future we imagined.
Sometimes grace opens our eyes to the provision of God in the middle of the future we never wanted.
Hagar filled the skin with water.
She gave the boy a drink.
And then Genesis says something astonishingly simple:
וַיְהִי אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הַנַּעַר
Vayehi Elohim et-hanna‘ar.
“God was with the boy.”
The household was gone.
Abraham was no longer beside him.
The water had failed.
The wilderness surrounded him.
But God was with the boy.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this desperately needed tonight.
People can leave you and God can still be with you.
A chapter can close and God can still be with you.
Your plans can collapse and God can still be with you.
You can carry scars from other people's decisions and God can still be with you.
You can carry consequences from your own decisions and discover that repentance and grace are still real.
But we must be careful here.
Genesis 21 is not teaching that every painful separation is automatically God's will.
It is not permission to abandon responsibilities and then call the consequences “God's plan.”
And Hagar's story is not a sentimental slogan telling wounded people that suffering does not matter.
Scripture is much more honest than that.
Sin has consequences.
Human impatience has consequences.
Family dysfunction has consequences.
Trying to accomplish God's purposes by sinful or faithless shortcuts has consequences.
Yet human failure does not place people beyond the reach of divine mercy.
And that brings us somewhere even greater than Abraham's wilderness.
It brings us to Jesus Christ.
Because the Bible's great story is not about wounded people eventually becoming strong enough to rescue themselves.
It is about a holy God rescuing sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Abraham could not save humanity.
Isaac could not save humanity.
Israel could not save humanity.
You cannot save yourself.
Neither can I.
The deepest wilderness is not financial difficulty, loneliness, betrayal, rejection, or heartbreak.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have sinned against the God who made us.
And no amount of religious performance can purchase our reconciliation with Him.
But God did not leave humanity beneath the shrub waiting to die.
He came for us.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He touched the rejected.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He carried the cross.
And on that cross, He bore sin.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
Then He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is the Gospel.
Not “try harder.”
Not “become religious enough.”
Not “hide your scandal well enough that Christians will accept you.”
Jesus saves sinners.
Grace does not pretend your past never happened.
Grace declares that your past does not have to possess the final word.
Repentance is not pretending the wilderness was beautiful.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy is greater than your rebellion.
Faith is not trusting your ability to repair yourself.
Faith is trusting Jesus Christ.
This is why the Gospel reaches so deeply into stories like Hagar's.
The Bible is full of messy families.
Broken people.
Shameful decisions.
Betrayals.
Failures.
Outcasts.
Sinners.
People who ran.
People who doubted.
People who fell.
People who discovered that God was still writing when they thought their story had ended.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe everybody thinks you are okay.
But you know about the wilderness.
You know about that thing you never discuss.
You know about the nights when the room becomes quiet and your memories become loud.
You know what you did.
You know what they did to you.
You know what you lost.
You know what you are afraid might never return.
And perhaps you have wondered:
“Could Jesus possibly want somebody with a story like mine?”
Look at the cross.
Christ did not die for imaginary people with spotless histories.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15).
Bring Him the real story.
Not the edited testimony.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
The real one.
Confess your sin.
Stop defending what God is asking you to surrender.
Stop hiding what Christ already knows.
Turn to Him.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is mercy in Jesus.
There is reconciliation with God in Jesus.
There is a new life in Jesus.
And there are people reading this right now who need permission to stop pretending.
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around our hearts.
Someone reading your two words may stop and pray.
Someone else may realize they are not alone.
And perhaps the wilderness that convinced you nobody could understand will become the place where somebody else finally finds courage to seek Jesus.
That is why this message should not stop with you.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that they are seen.
God hears.

We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ—through faith, obedience, love, generosity, service, witness, and worship. Supporting Gospel ministry can be one expression of that devotion when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for the sake of Christ rather than human recognition.
But the greater invitation is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is feeding your soul instead of endlessly feeding your distractions.
Share Christ.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Send this to the person who thinks their scandal has disqualified them from grace.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling Christians.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Because somewhere tonight, another Hagar is crying.
Somewhere, another person believes the water is gone and therefore hope must be gone too.
Somewhere, someone has mistaken a wilderness chapter for the final page.
But Genesis 21 whispers across thousands of years:
God heard.
God opened her eyes.
God provided.
God was with the boy.
And the whole testimony of Scripture ultimately leads us beyond a well in Beersheba to the Savior who said:
“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).
Bread runs out.
Water skins become empty.
Human strength collapses.
People disappoint us.
Earthly security disappears.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So when your wilderness tells you, “This is where your story dies,” remember the God who hears.
When shame tells you, “Nobody could love you if they knew everything,” remember the cross.
When sin tells you, “You have gone too far,” remember the Savior who calls sinners to repent and come home.
When yesterday tells you, “Your scandal is your identity,” remember grace.
And when you cannot see the next chapter, remember this:
The wilderness may expose everything you have lost, but it can never erase the God who hears your cry—and in Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence.
Somewhere between the empty water skin and the opened well, despair discovered that God had been listening all along.
